upper_bound.quote: They lie in $(0,1)$, so their $2^{n+1}-3$ consecutive gaps sum to less than $1$. When put in nondecreasing order, two consecutive subset sums therefore differ by at most
upper_bound.witness: COUNTEREXAMPLE/NON-SEQUITUR. From 2^{n+1}-3 gaps summing to <1 one only gets a minimal gap < 1/(2^{n+1}-3), which exceeds d=1/(2^{n+1}-1); the stated conclusion does not follow. Moreover it is false: take n=1, Liu's intervals a_1=0.9, a_2=0.1 (m=n+1=2). The only nonempty proper subsets are {1},{2}, with sums 0.9 and 0.1; the single gap is 0.8 > 1/3 = d. So no two nonempty proper subset sums differ by at most d, and (12) with A={1},B={2} gives |0.9-0.1|=0.8, leaving unpaired material 0.8, not ≤ d. The standard fix (including S=∅ and S=full set, giving 2^{n+1} sums in [0,1] and 2^{n+1}-1 gaps summing to 1) is not what is written.
upper_bound.load_bearing: Every branch of Section 5 (the empty-A/B case and the common-refinement case) derives D ≤ d only from the bound (12), which is obtained solely from this gap estimate; without it the residual unpaired length is uncontrolled.

parsed.notes: Reduction (alternating sum via backward induction) and the pairing/tree lower bound with 1:2:...:2^n are complete and correct. The upper bound's pigeonhole uses only nonempty proper subsets (2^{n+1}-3 gaps), which cannot yield the bound 1/(2^{n+1}-1); explicit counterexample at n=1.
